study_type_evidence.quote: Rat and mouse blood was drawn from the heart, under halothane aesthesia, by cardiac puncture into heparinized tubes.
1 ml aliquots of blood were incubated in a water bath at 37 °C for 5 min and 20 μl of the [3H]-THF solution ... was added
study_type_evidence.section: METHODS / Preparation and incubation of the samples

ex_vivo_detail: Whole heparinized blood from three species, incubated with radiolabelled peptide at 37 C. Animal blood: male Wistar rats (180-200 g) and male Laca mice (35-40 g), fasted overnight with free access to water, bled from the heart by cardiac puncture under halothane anaesthesia; blood from three different rats or mice was used as separate samples in each study. Human blood: drawn into heparinized tubes from three healthy male blood donors. Peptidase-inhibitor experiments (amastatin, 1,10-phenanthroline, phosphoramidon, AEBSF, EDTA, 1,7-phenanthroline, PMSF) were performed in human blood only.

concentration_time_figure.locator: Fig. 1A (rat blood), Fig. 1B (mouse blood), Fig. 2 (human blood); also Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 showing the fitted/simulated time courses
concentration_time_figure.caption_quote: Time-course of the degradation of THF-γ2 on incubation with rat and mouse blood. A) Time-course with rat blood. B) Time-course with mouse blood.
concentration_time_figure.note: Percentage of total peptide (intact THF-gamma2 and each degradation fragment) plotted against incubation time from 0 to 60 min at 37 C in mouse, rat and human whole blood; sampling at 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45 and 60 min. This is a %-remaining versus time whole-blood stability profile. Each point is mean +/- SEM of 3 independent determinations. Fig. 5 overlays the Laplace-transform analytical solution on the human data and Fig. 6 shows the numerically integrated rat/mouse model.

bioanalytical_method: Radio-thin-layer chromatography: silica gel plates developed in water-methanol-acetic acid-chloroform (6:14:20:40 v/v), gel scraped in 1 cm sections and quantified by liquid scintillation counting (Soluene-350 / Hionic-Fluor), with unlabelled synthetic fragment peptides as Rf markers; samples first deproteinised with ice-cold acetonitrile and extracted with dichloromethane
bioanalytical_quote: Separations were carried out on Silica gel plates (Merk-Millipore F254) ... the gel was scraped from 1 cm sections into scintillation vials containing 1 ml Soluene-350. 10 ml Hionic-Fluor was then added for liquid scintillation counting.
notes: No animal or human was dosed in this study; the peptide was added to blood after collection, so this is entirely an ex vivo whole-blood degradation study and in_vivo_species is an empty array. ex_vivo_origin is recorded as 'human and animal' because both human donor blood and rodent blood were used; the protocol's single-value field cannot represent this. The PeplLife2 metadata labels the row 'In Vitro' and gives the assay as 'N.A.'; the actual assay described in the body is radio-TLC with liquid scintillation counting, not a chromatographic UV method. The PeplLife2 half-life of 5.6 +/- 0.2 min in mouse blood matches the body exactly. NOTE an internal inconsistency in the source: the Results section gives the human whole-blood half-life as 5.2 +/- 0.4 min, whereas the Discussion states 'a half-life of less than 4 min' for human whole blood; both figures are in the body and neither has been altered here. The ~12 min half-life in human plasma is cited from earlier work (Bramucci et al.), not measured here. There is also an apparent arithmetic inconsistency in the Methods between the stated 30 ng of labelled peptide added to 1 mL of blood and the stated final concentration of 93 nmol/mL; both values are quoted verbatim without correction. Rate constants for the rat/mouse model are given in the Fig. 6 caption (k1 = 0.15, k2 = 0.02, k3 = 0.08, k4 = 0.05, k5 = 0.025, k6 = 0.25, k7 = 0.03, k8 = 0.2, k9 = 0.0, k10 = 0.01 min^-1; A0 = 88.0). Mouse blood produced only two major fragments (2-8 and 2-6) versus three (2-8, 3-8, 2-6) in rat and human blood, and the authors conclude 'mouse would appear to be a less satisfactory model for the proteolysis in blood than the rat'.
